question: According to the South Carolina CDL Manual, what is responsible for more than half of truck driver deaths in crashes?
choice_a: Rollovers
choice_c: Head-on collisions
choice_d: Brake fires
explanation: The manual states that more than half of truck driver deaths in crashes are the result of truck rollovers.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.1.1, Rollover Risks

question: How does adding more cargo affect a truck's rollover risk, according to the manual?
choice_a: It lowers the center of gravity
choice_b: It raises the center of gravity, making the truck easier to roll over
choice_c: It has no effect on rollover risk
choice_d: It only affects braking distance
explanation: The manual explains that when more cargo is piled up in a truck, the center of gravity moves higher up from the road, making the truck easier to turn over.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.1.1, Rollover Risks

question: Fully loaded rigs are how many times more likely to roll over in a crash than empty rigs, per the manual?
choice_a: Two times
choice_c: Ten times
choice_d: Twenty times
explanation: The manual states that fully loaded rigs are ten times more likely to roll over in a crash than empty rigs.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.1.1, Rollover Risks

question: Why should you steer gently and smoothly when pulling trailers?
choice_a: It improves fuel economy
choice_c: It is required only in bad weather
choice_d: A sudden steering movement can cause the trailer to tip over
explanation: The manual warns that if you make a sudden movement with your steering wheel while pulling trailers, your trailer could tip over.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.1, Driving Combination Vehicles Safely

question: In addition to at least 1 second of following distance for each 10 feet of vehicle length, what extra allowance does the manual recommend?
choice_a: An additional second if traveling over 40 mph
choice_b: An extra 2 seconds in any traffic
choice_c: An additional 5 seconds at night
choice_d: Double the distance in rain
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to follow at least 1 second for each 10 feet of vehicle length, plus another second if going over 40 mph.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.1, Driving Combination Vehicles Safely

question: When do large combination vehicles take longer to stop, according to the manual?
choice_a: Fully loaded
choice_c: Stopping distance is the same either way
choice_d: It depends only on tire tread
explanation: The manual states that large combination vehicles take longer to stop when they are empty than when they are fully loaded.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.1.3, Brake Early

question: Why is it easy to lock up the wheels when a combination vehicle is lightly loaded?
choice_a: The brakes are weaker when empty
choice_b: The trailer has no brakes when empty
choice_c: Stiff suspension springs and strong brakes give poor traction
choice_d: ABS is disabled when unloaded
explanation: When lightly loaded, the very stiff suspension springs and strong brakes give poor traction and make it very easy to lock up the wheels.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.1.3, Brake Early

question: What does the manual say about driving "bobtail" tractors (tractors without semitrailers)?
choice_a: They stop more quickly than loaded rigs
choice_b: They are not permitted on public roads
choice_c: They require lower following distances
choice_d: Tests show they can be very hard to stop smoothly and take longer to stop than a tractor-semitrailer loaded to maximum gross weight
explanation: The manual notes tests have shown that bobtails can be very hard to stop smoothly, and it takes them longer to stop than a tractor-semitrailer loaded to maximum gross weight.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.1.3, Brake Early

question: What is a particular hazard for combination vehicles at railroad-highway crossings?
choice_a: Low underneath clearance trailers can get stuck on raised crossings
choice_b: All trailers must stop before crossing
choice_c: ABS must be disengaged before crossing
choice_d: Glad hands must be disconnected
explanation: The manual lists trailers such as lowboys, car carriers, moving vans, and possum-belly livestock trailers that can get stuck on raised railroad crossings due to low underneath clearance.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.1.4, Railroad-highway Crossings

question: If you get stuck on railroad tracks, what should you do first, according to the manual?
choice_a: Try to drive forward off the tracks quickly
choice_b: Get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks, then call 911
choice_c: Stay in the vehicle and honk the horn
choice_d: Wait for the train to pass before moving
explanation: The manual instructs that if you get stuck on the tracks, get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks, then call 911 or another emergency number with the crossing location.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.1.4, Railroad-highway Crossings

question: What is the earliest and best way to recognize that a trailer has started to skid?
choice_a: Feeling the steering wheel vibrate
choice_c: Seeing it in your mirrors
choice_d: Noticing the speedometer drop
explanation: The manual states the earliest and best way to recognize a trailer skid is by seeing it in your mirrors, especially any time you apply the brakes hard.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.1.5, Prevent Trailer Skids

question: What should you do to stop a trailer skid once you recognize it?
choice_a: Apply the trailer hand brake to straighten the rig
choice_b: Accelerate to pull the trailer straight
choice_c: Turn the steering wheel sharply into the skid
choice_d: Release the brakes to get traction back
explanation: The procedure for stopping a trailer skid includes releasing the brakes to get traction back, allowing the trailer wheels to grip the road again and follow the tractor.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.1.5, Prevent Trailer Skids

question: Why should you not use the trailer hand brake to try to straighten out a jackknifing trailer?
choice_a: The brakes on the trailer wheels caused the skid in the first place, so using the hand brake is the wrong thing to do
choice_b: It has no effect on the trailer at all
choice_c: It will only work on downhill grades
choice_d: It disconnects the tractor protection valve
explanation: The manual explains this is the wrong thing to do because the brakes on the trailer wheels caused the skid in the first place.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.1.5, Prevent Trailer Skids

question: What is the term for the rear wheels of a vehicle following a different, tighter path than the front wheels when turning?
choice_a: Rearward amplification
choice_c: Trailer sway
choice_d: Drift
explanation: The manual calls this off-tracking or "cheating," noting it causes the path followed by a tractor to be wider than the rig itself.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.1.6, Turn Wide

question: In a combination vehicle with more than one trailer, which wheels off-track the most?
choice_a: The rear wheels of the powered unit (tractor)
choice_b: The rear wheels of the first trailer
choice_c: The rear wheels of the last trailer
choice_d: The front steering wheels
explanation: The manual states that if there is more than one trailer, the rear wheels of the last trailer will off-track the most.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.1.6, Turn Wide

question: When completing a turn without entering another traffic lane, what technique does the manual recommend?
choice_a: Swing wide to the left before starting the turn
choice_c: Cut the corner sharply to minimize off-tracking
choice_d: Turn wide as you complete the turn, keeping the rear close to the curb
explanation: The manual recommends turning wide as you complete the turn (rather than swinging wide to the left before starting), which keeps other drivers from passing you on the right.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.1.6, Turn Wide

question: When backing a trailer, which direction do you turn the steering wheel, relative to backing a car, straight truck, or bus?
choice_a: The opposite direction
choice_c: It does not matter
choice_d: You should not turn the wheel at all
explanation: The manual states that when backing a trailer, you turn the steering wheel in the opposite direction from how you would when backing a car, straight truck, or bus.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.1.7, Backing with a Trailer

question: If you must back on a curved path, to which side should you back, per the manual?
choice_a: The passenger's side
choice_b: The driver's side, so you can see
choice_c: Either side is equally recommended
choice_d: Straight back only, curves are not allowed
explanation: The manual advises that if you must back on a curved path, back to the driver's side so you can see.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.1.7, Backing with a Trailer

question: What does the manual recommend if you see the trailer getting off the proper path while backing?
choice_a: Continue and correct at the end
choice_c: Correct the drift immediately by turning the top of the steering wheel in the direction of the drift
choice_d: Apply the trailer hand brake
explanation: The manual instructs to correct drift immediately as soon as you see the trailer getting off the proper path, by turning the top of the steering wheel in the direction of the drift.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.1.7, Backing with a Trailer

question: What is the trailer hand valve (also called the trolley valve or Johnson bar) meant to be used for?
choice_a: Normal driving braking
choice_c: Releasing the tractor protection valve
choice_d: Only to test the trailer brakes
explanation: The manual states the trailer hand valve should be used only to test the trailer brakes, not in driving, because of the danger of making the trailer skid.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.2.1, Trailer Hand Valve

question: Why should the trailer hand valve never be used for parking?
choice_a: All the air might leak out, unlocking the brakes in trailers without spring brakes
choice_c: It automatically disconnects the glad hands
choice_d: It triggers the ABS malfunction lamp
explanation: The manual warns never to use the hand valve for parking because all the air might leak out, unlocking the brakes in trailers that don't have spring brakes; the parking brakes should always be used instead.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.2.1, Trailer Hand Valve

question: What does the tractor protection valve do if the trailer breaks away or develops a bad leak?
choice_a: It releases all air from the tractor system
choice_b: It keeps air in the tractor or truck brake system
choice_c: It locks the fifth wheel
choice_d: It shuts off the trailer's electrical system
explanation: The manual states the tractor protection valve keeps air in the tractor or truck brake system should the trailer break away or develop a bad leak.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.2.2, Tractor Protection Valve

question: In what air pressure range will the tractor protection valve automatically close, per the manual?
choice_a: 5 to 15 psi
choice_c: 20 to 45 psi
choice_d: 80 to 100 psi
explanation: The manual states the tractor protection valve will close automatically if air pressure is low, in the range of 20 to 45 psi.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.2.2, Tractor Protection Valve

question: What color and shape is the trailer air supply control knob on newer vehicles?
choice_a: A blue round knob
choice_c: A green triangular knob
choice_d: A red eight-sided knob
explanation: The manual describes the trailer air supply control on newer vehicles as a red eight-sided knob used to control the tractor protection valve.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.2.3, Trailer Air Supply Control

question: What happens when you pull out the trailer air supply control knob?
choice_a: It shuts the air off and puts on the trailer emergency brakes
choice_b: It supplies the trailer with air
choice_c: It releases the parking brakes
choice_d: It activates the ABS system
explanation: The manual states you push the knob in to supply the trailer with air, and pull it out to shut the air off and put on the trailer emergency brakes.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.2.3, Trailer Air Supply Control

question: What are the two air-lines found on every combination vehicle?
choice_a: The primary line and secondary line
choice_b: The service line and the emergency line
choice_c: The parking line and driving line
choice_d: The relay line and signal line
explanation: The manual states that every combination vehicle has two air-lines: the service line and the emergency line, running between each vehicle in the combination.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.2.4, Trailer Air-lines

question: What are the two purposes of the emergency line (also called the supply line)?
choice_a: It only powers the ABS computer
choice_c: It supplies air to the trailer air tanks and controls the emergency brakes
choice_d: It only operates the fifth wheel release
explanation: The manual explains the emergency line has two purposes: it supplies air to the trailer air tanks and controls the emergency brakes on combination vehicles.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.2.4, Trailer Air-lines

question: What is the purpose of the rubber seal in glad hand couplers?
choice_a: To reduce noise
choice_c: To indicate low tire pressure
choice_d: To prevent air from escaping
explanation: The manual states glad hands have a rubber seal, which prevents air from escaping, and that couplers and seals should be cleaned before connecting.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.2.5, Hose Couplers (Glad Hands)

question: What color is typically used for the service air-line versus the emergency air-line, per the manual?
choice_a: Blue for service, red for emergency
choice_b: Red for service, blue for emergency
choice_c: Green for service, yellow for emergency
choice_d: Black for service, white for emergency
explanation: The manual notes that colors are sometimes used to avoid mistakes: blue is used for the service lines and red for the emergency (supply) lines.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.2.5, Hose Couplers (Glad Hands)

question: How are trailer and converter dolly air tanks filled?
choice_a: By the service line from the tractor
choice_b: By the emergency (supply) line from the tractor
choice_c: By a manual hand pump
choice_d: By the ABS computer
explanation: The manual states each trailer and converter dolly has one or more air tanks, filled by the emergency (supply) line from the tractor.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.2.6, Trailer Air Tanks

question: Why is it important not to let water and oil build up in air tanks?
choice_a: It can cause rust that voids the warranty
choice_b: It triggers the ABS malfunction lamp
choice_c: The brakes may not work correctly
choice_d: It reduces fuel economy
explanation: The manual warns that if water and oil build up in the air tanks, the brakes may not work correctly, so each tank should be drained every day.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.2.6, Trailer Air Tanks

question: What are shut-off valves (also called cut-out cocks) used for?
choice_a: To disconnect the electrical cord
choice_c: To adjust tire pressure
choice_d: To permit closing the air-lines off when another trailer is not being towed
explanation: The manual states shut-off valves are used in the service and supply air-lines at the back of trailers used to tow other trailers, permitting the air-lines to be closed off when another trailer is not being towed.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.2.7, Shut-off Valves

question: On the last trailer in a combination, how should the shut-off valves at the very back be positioned?
choice_a: Closed
choice_c: Half-open
choice_d: It does not matter
explanation: The manual instructs that you must check that all shut-off valves are in the open position except the ones at the back of the last trailer, which must be closed.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.2.7, Shut-off Valves

topic: Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes
question: Which trailers and converter dollies are NOT required to have spring brakes, per the manual?
choice_a: All trailers built after 1990
choice_b: Converter dollies and trailers built before 1975
choice_c: Only trailers used for triples
choice_d: Only trailers with ABS
explanation: The manual states that converter dollies and trailers built before 1975 are not required to have spring brakes; those without spring brakes instead have emergency brakes.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.2.8, Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes

topic: Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes
question: Why is it important to use wheel chocks when parking trailers without spring brakes?
choice_a: Because they have no brakes of any kind
choice_b: Because chocks are legally required regardless of brake type
choice_c: Because their emergency brakes only hold as long as there is air pressure in the trailer air tank, which will eventually leak away
choice_d: Because chocks improve fuel economy
explanation: The manual explains that emergency brakes on such trailers hold only as long as there is air pressure in the trailer air tank; eventually the air will leak away and there will be no brakes, so wheel chocks are important for safety.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.2.8, Trailer Service, Parking and Emergency Brakes

question: As of what date are all trailers and converter dollies required to have ABS, per the manual?
choice_a: January 1, 1995
choice_c: December 1, 2005
choice_d: March 1, 1998
explanation: The manual states all trailers and converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998, are required to have ABS.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.3.1, Trailers Required to Have ABS

question: What color are the ABS malfunction lamps on trailers, and where are they located?
choice_a: Yellow, on the left side (front or rear corner)
choice_c: Blue, on the rear door
choice_d: Green, on the roof
explanation: The manual states trailers will have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the left side, either on the front or rear corner.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.3.1, Trailers Required to Have ABS

question: Does ABS decrease or increase a vehicle's normal braking capability, according to the manual?
choice_a: It significantly increases braking capability
choice_b: It is only an addition to normal brakes and does not decrease or increase normal braking capability
choice_c: It significantly decreases braking capability
choice_d: It replaces the normal brakes entirely
explanation: The manual states ABS is an addition to your normal brakes and does not decrease or increase your normal braking capability; it only activates when wheels are about to lock up.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.3.2, Braking with ABS

question: According to the manual, how should you brake when driving a tractor-trailer combination with ABS?
choice_a: Brake much harder immediately
choice_c: Brake the same way regardless of whether you have ABS on the tractor, trailer, or both
choice_d: Pump the brakes rapidly at all times
explanation: The manual instructs that you should brake the same way regardless of whether you have ABS on the tractor, the trailer, or both, using only the braking force necessary to stop safely.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.3.2, Braking with ABS

question: During Step 1 (Inspect Fifth Wheel) of coupling a tractor-semitrailer, what could result from failing to keep the fifth wheel plate lubricated?
choice_a: Faster brake wear
choice_c: Electrical short circuits
choice_d: Steering problems because of friction between tractor and trailer
explanation: The manual warns that failure to keep the fifth wheel plate lubricated could cause steering problems because of friction between the tractor and trailer.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.4.1, Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: When positioning the tractor to couple with a trailer, why should you never back under the trailer at an angle?
choice_a: It could push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear
choice_c: It triggers the tractor protection valve
choice_d: It voids the manufacturer's warranty
explanation: The manual states you should never back under the trailer at an angle because you might push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.4.1, Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: What should the trailer height be before backing the tractor under it, per Step 6 of coupling?
choice_a: As high as possible
choice_b: Low enough that it is raised slightly by the tractor when backed under it
choice_c: Exactly level with the tractor frame
choice_d: It doesn't matter as long as the kingpin aligns
explanation: The manual states the trailer should be low enough that it is raised slightly by the tractor when the tractor is backed under it, and to raise or lower the trailer as needed.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.4.1, Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: After connecting the air-lines and supplying air to the trailer (Step 8), why should you shut the engine off before checking the brakes?
choice_a: To save fuel
choice_b: It is required by DOT regulation before every test
choice_c: So you can hear the brakes being applied and released
choice_d: To prevent the ABS from engaging
explanation: The manual instructs to shut the engine off so you can hear the brakes, then apply and release the trailer brakes to listen for the sound of them being applied and released.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.4.1, Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: After backing under the trailer and locking the kingpin into the fifth wheel, how do you check the connection for security (Step 11)?
choice_a: Visually inspect from a distance only
choice_b: Drive at normal speed and observe
choice_c: Disconnect the air-lines and reconnect them
choice_d: Raise the trailer landing gear slightly and pull the tractor gently forward while the trailer brakes are locked
explanation: The manual instructs to raise the trailer landing gear slightly off the ground and pull the tractor gently forward while the trailer brakes are still locked to check that the trailer is locked onto the tractor.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.4.1, Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: During the final coupling inspection, what does visible space between the upper and lower fifth wheel indicate?
choice_a: Something is wrong -- the kingpin may be on top of the closed fifth wheel jaws and the trailer could come loose easily
choice_c: The landing gear needs to be raised
choice_d: The glad hands are not connected properly
explanation: The manual warns that if there is space between the upper and lower fifth wheel, something is wrong -- the kingpin may be on top of the closed fifth wheel jaws, and the trailer would come loose very easily.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.4.1, Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: Before uncoupling, what should you check about the parking area surface?
choice_a: That it is painted with lane markings
choice_b: That the surface can support the weight of the trailer
choice_c: That it is within 100 feet of a fuel pump
choice_d: That it has a loading dock
explanation: The manual's Step 1 (Position Rig) for uncoupling instructs to make sure the surface of the parking area can support the weight of the trailer.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.4.2, Uncoupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: When uncoupling, why should you ease pressure on the fifth wheel locking jaws by backing up gently while the parking brakes hold the rig against the kingpin?
choice_a: It disconnects the electrical cord automatically
choice_c: It helps release the fifth wheel locking lever
choice_d: It raises the landing gear automatically
explanation: The manual explains that easing pressure on the fifth wheel locking jaws by backing up gently will help you release the fifth wheel locking lever.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.4.2, Uncoupling Tractor-Semitrailers

question: What could happen if the pintle hook is not securely mounted to the mounting surface?
choice_a: Only minor cosmetic damage
choice_c: The ABS malfunction lamp would illuminate
choice_d: The pintle hook could separate from the vehicle, which if not avoided could result in death or serious injury
explanation: The manual states that if the pintle hook is not secured to the mounting surface, it could separate from the vehicle, which if not avoided could result in death or serious injury.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.4.3, Coupling a Pintle Hook

question: When lowering the drawbar into place on a pintle hook, where should the drawbar eye be positioned?
choice_a: Over the horn of the pintle hook
choice_c: Under the kingpin
choice_d: Beside the glad hands
explanation: The manual instructs to position the drawbar eye over the horn of the pintle hook and lower it into place.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.4.3, Coupling a Pintle Hook

question: Before uncoupling a pintle hook trailer, what must you disconnect in addition to the electrical connector and safety chains?
choice_a: The fifth wheel release handle
choice_c: The ABS sensor wires
choice_d: The drawbar coupling ball
explanation: The manual's uncoupling steps for a pintle hook list disconnecting the electrical connector, the breakaway brake switch lanyard, and the safety chains from the tow vehicle.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.4.4, Uncoupling a Pintle Hook

question: When reversing the truck to couple a drawbar, where should the ball cup drawbar eye be positioned?
choice_a: Several inches to the side of the ball
choice_c: Exactly above the drawbar coupling ball
choice_d: At a 45-degree angle to the ball

question: What vertical clearance should be set between the guard disk and the ball cup when adjusting the adjustment screw on a drawbar coupling?

question: Before latching the clamp on a Gooseneck hitch coupler, what should you make sure of regarding the Gooseneck ball?

question: During the walk-around inspection of the lower fifth wheel, where should the locking jaws be positioned?
choice_a: Around the head of the kingpin

question: When inspecting the air and electric lines to the trailer, what should you check regarding slack?
choice_a: Lines should have no slack at all

choice_c: Slack is only relevant for triples

choice_b: That it is positioned as far forward as mechanically possible

question: How do you test that air flows to all trailers during a brake check?
choice_a: Disconnect the glad hands and observe air pressure drop
choice_b: Open the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer and listen for air escaping, showing the system is charged
choice_c: Drive the vehicle at highway speed
choice_d: Check only the dashboard gauge
explanation: The manual instructs to open the emergency line shut-off valve at the rear of the last trailer; hearing air escaping shows the entire system is charged, then the valve is closed and the service line valve is checked the same way.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.5.2, Combination Vehicle Brake Check

question: How do you test the tractor protection valve, per the manual?
choice_a: Disconnect the trailer entirely and observe
choice_c: Charge the system, shut the engine off, and pump the brake pedal several times to reduce air pressure until the control pops out or moves to "emergency"
choice_d: Check the ABS malfunction lamp
explanation: The manual instructs to charge the air-brake system, push the air supply knob in, shut the engine off, and step on and off the brake pedal several times until the trailer air supply control pops out or moves to the emergency position at the specified pressure range.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.5.2, Combination Vehicle Brake Check

question: How do you test the trailer service brakes, per the manual?
choice_a: Check that the trailer rolls freely with no brakes applied
choice_b: Pull the trailer air supply control and observe the ABS lamp
choice_c: Listen for air escaping at the glad hands only
choice_d: Release the parking brakes, move the vehicle forward slowly, and apply the trailer brakes with the hand control -- you should feel the brakes come on
explanation: The manual instructs to check for normal air pressure, release the parking brakes, move the vehicle forward slowly, and apply the trailer brakes with the hand control (trolley valve); you should feel the brakes come on, confirming they are connected and working.
source_note: South Carolina Commercial Driver License Manual (Version: March 2025, AAMVA 2005 CDL Testing System base content), South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV) -- Section 6.5.2, Combination Vehicle Brake Check
